narrative:
The model determined that you have an 80% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk of failure is so high, the law school decided to reject your application.

Three factors drove this outcome more than anything else. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence, followed by your class ranking in the third year of law school, then your first-year ranking. In each case the model saw values that strongly pushed the prediction toward failure rather than success.

Your LSAT score of 19 sits far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling much weaker preparation for the exam. Similarly, finishing in the bottom decile for both your first-year and third-year grades placed you well behind the typical accepted student, who ranked around the middle of their class. These academic signals together created a clear picture for the model that the odds of passing the bar were low.

Gender and race played no role in the decision. Family income and plans to attend full-time were also far less important than your test score and grades.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score substantially through intensive preparation, and consider strengthening your academic record if you retake any coursework. These steps would directly address the factors that led to the rejection.
